newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albanian PM rebuffs rebels, but offers dialogue.
newsitem.headline: Albanian PM rebuffs rebels, but offers dialogue.

text.p: Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino on Saturday rebuffed rebels holding the south of the country by dismissing their calls for President Sali Berisha to quit but said he was ready to open a dialogue with them.

In an interview with Reuters, Fino said Berisha's resignation would cause a power vacuum in a country still reeling from weeks of looting and shooting by Albanians angry at the loss of their money in failed savings schemes.
Berisha himself, in a rare public statement, called on Albanians to work together to resolve the current crisis.

"All Albanians should overcome the situation and look towards the future...We have not lost our trust in the future, our trust in democracy or in the European orientation of the country, which remain fundamental principles."

Fino said his all-party government appointed earlier this month had more pressing tasks than trying to force out Berisha, in particular restoring order, distributing humanitarian aid and preparing for elections in June.

Fino, a member of the opposition Socialist Party, has been locked in a power struggle with Berisha's Democrats, who control 122 of the 140 seats in parliament after elections last May that international observers said were deeply flawed.
"The government has a more important mission than asking for the president's resignation," Fino said. "It would create an institutional vacuum if Berisha were to resign."
Leaders of most political parties represented in the government have made it clear they want an end to Berisha's presidency, but would prefer this was brought about by democratic means.
Berisha, blamed by the rebels for not stopping the shady savings schemes, has promised to quit if his party loses new elections to be held by June.

Fino was speaking a day after rebel leaders from 14 towns in southern Albania issued a fresh call for Berisha to resign, but pulled back from a confrontation with the government by dropping plans to set up a rival leadership in the south.

On Saturday Fino had a meeting with rebel leaders from the southern port of Vlore, a focal point of the uprising, and according to state television appealed to them to act responsibly at a time when the territorial integrity of the country had become an imperative.
The premier said dialogue rather than ultimatums was crucial for getting the country back to normal.
Participants at the meeting promised Fino they would stabilise the situation in Vlore so it could serve as an example for the whole country, television reported.

Vlore, along with other rebel-held towns in the south, is ostensibly under the control of citizens' councils but there is widespread lawlessness following the looting of weapons from army depots at the start of the revolt.

Italy was preparing to send emergency health supplies to Albania at the weekend following a request from Fino. The Foreign Ministry in Rome said the supplies, in the form of health kits, would be enough for 300,000 people for a month.
No aid had arrived on Saturday morning, although an Italian air force transport plane flew in a further group of "undesirable" Albanian refugees expelled from Italy.
European Union foreign ministers are due to meet on Monday in Brussels to provide a blueprint for security measures to assist a major humanitarian relief mission in the wake of the unrest.
